Composition Jungle Gym · 0.48 · for Justin

Two decisions to see

Decision 5, the solfa ladder on phones, and Decision 12, a colour for minor v and VII. Everything shown is measured from the mock-ups in this folder.

5

The solfa ladder on phones

Melodic dictation, rung 3, E minor, four notes written. A 390 × 844 phone in Safari with its bars showing, which leaves 664 px for the page.

A correction to my spec first. I wrote that 44 px rows would be “up from 24”. That was wrong. The app’s 24 px is a grid track and each note spans two, so the ladder you have now already has 47 px rows: 384 px tall at rung 3 (8 notes), 432 px at rung 2 (9 notes), measured in the running app at 390 px. So A is close to what ships today, and B would be a new, smaller ladder, not a return to 0.47.

C

Two columns

8 notes · rows 47 px · ladder 216 px tall
9:41
Composition Jungle Gym
  • Tap accuracy Full-size targets, 47 × 161 px, each half a row above the next.
  • Scrolling None. Ladder, Undo and Clear all show at once.
  • Stave and ladder Costs the single column: the eye zigzags, steps cross the gap and thirds stack (m–d–l, on the left). New to every student; “home” has less room.

Keeps the targets and loses the height. Worth building only if scrolling proves a problem in class.

Recommendation

A. Keep the single column at full height. It is the tone ladder students already sing from, the targets are safe, and the cost is one short scroll for the bottom two notes while the browser bars are up. Once the bars tuck away (about 80 px more) this eight-note ladder fits whole; the nine-note ladder at rung 2 still needs a short scroll unless the app is opened from the home screen. Check is always in reach in the dock. Nothing in the app has to change: the 47 px rows it has now already meet the rule, and I will correct the spec. Hold C in reserve: it is the only way to get full targets with no scroll, but it changes the picture of the ladder, so it should be your call as the Kodály teacher, not a layout fix I slip in.

Numerals under the SATB scores take the colour of their function. In a minor key, v and VII have no leading note, so they are not dominant red. They were blue-grey #7fb3c8, which you turned down. Three others, each next to the four you have.

Recommendation

1. Madder rose #bd6b97, deepened to #9e4776 on ivory. It sits beside the dominant’s red as its cooler relative, which is the theory: same region of the key, without the semitone pull. It clears 4.5 : 1 on every ground and stays apart from the other four for all three kinds of colour-blindness. Verdigris measures a little further apart, but it is the nearest thing here to the blue-grey you rejected. Shell fails for a different reason: beside ivory text it stops looking like a category.

What to call it

“Modal dominant”, short code MD, with the plain word “soft pull” to sit beside home, away and pull. It says what the chords are (built on the dominant side of the key, from the unraised 7th) without claiming one school’s label. The note behind it can name the traditions: function theory calls v the minor dominant and VII its relative; many English-language texts call VII the subtonic chord; in modal, folk and rock harmony the two are the ordinary closing chords. Second choice: “subtonic chords”.

ΔE is CIEDE2000 between the candidate and its nearest neighbour among the four, after simulating each kind of colour-blindness (Machado et al. 2009, full severity); above about 10 two colours are easy to tell apart. For scale, the old blue-grey scored ΔE 7. Two things about the existing four turned up on the way and are outside this decision: tonic green and predominant gold are only ΔE 5 apart under deuteranopia, and dominant red is 3.9 : 1 on the darkest panel, under the 4.5 line. The numerals differ by their letters as well, so neither blocks 0.48.
